title: The Traditional Story of Ganpati's Birth
text: According to tradition, Goddess Parvati created Ganesha from turmeric or sandalwood paste to stand guard while she bathed, instructing him to let no one enter. When Lord Shiva returned and was refused entry by the boy he didn't recognize, a fight broke out and Shiva severed the boy's head. Parvati's grief moved Shiva to restore him to life, and since the original head could not be found, an elephant's head was placed on the child instead — giving Ganesha his familiar form. He was named leader (Gana-pati) of Shiva's attendants.

title: Why Ganpati Is Worshipped First
text: Ganesha is traditionally invoked before any other deity or new undertaking. One well-known story explains this with a race: Ganesha's parents, Shiva and Parvati, offered a fruit to whichever of their two sons — Ganesha or Kartikeya — could circle the universe first. Kartikeya set off travelling the physical world, while Ganesha simply walked around his parents, saying they were his whole universe. Pleased with his wisdom, Shiva and Parvati granted Ganesha the boon of being worshipped first (Prathama Pujya) before any ritual or new venture.

title: When Ganeshotsav Starts and Ends
text: Ganeshotsav begins on Bhadrapada Shukla Chaturthi, the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the Hindu month of Bhadrapada, and ends on Anant Chaturdashi, the fourteenth day of the same fortnight, when the idols are immersed (visarjan). This makes the festival 10 or 11 days long depending on the lunar calendar that year. Because it follows the Hindu lunisolar calendar, the exact Gregorian dates shift every year, usually falling between August and September.

title: History of Public Ganeshotsav
text: Ganpati has been worshipped privately in Maharashtrian households for centuries, but the public, community-wide celebration (Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav) was formally started in Pune in 1893 by Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak. Tilak encouraged installing large public idols and organizing community celebrations partly as a way to bring people together and build a shared sense of identity during British colonial rule, since large religious gatherings could not easily be banned. Kasba Ganpati, Pune's Gramdevata, was given the first ceremonial rank (first Manacha Ganpati) when this public tradition began.

title: Interesting Facts About Ganpati
text: Ganesha is known by many names, including Ganapati, Vinayaka, and Vighnaharta ('remover of obstacles'). His vehicle (vahana) is a mouse (mushak). He is usually shown holding a modak (a sweet dumpling), his favorite food. His broken tusk, used to write down the Mahabharata as sage Vyasa dictated it, is a common feature in depictions. In Pune specifically, the Manache Ganpati are five mandals given ceremonial precedence, ranked in a fixed order established when the public festival began in 1893.
